messages.content:
Slovenia is awesome.

Triglav National Park is cool, including Lake Bohinj. Lake Bled is beautiful, too -- gotta spend at least two nights there, especially because Vintgar Gorge is just 10-15 min drive away.

Predjama Castle is cool for sure. And I strongly recommend you hit at least one of the two major cave systems. My recommendation would be Skocjan, but lots of people like Postojna, too. My understanding is that Postojna is a little "easier" than Skocjan, but I thought Skocjan was the coolest cave system I've ever been to.

I agree with the other commenter that a full day is Ljubljana is probably enough.

I didn't have time to see this, but there's also a cool stable for...clydesdales? Some kind of spectacular horse, anyway. If you like horses you should check that out.

Enjoy! It's been 7-8 years, but I remember my visit like it was yesterday.

You'll have a blast. Here's how I'd do five nights:

Arrive, spend Night 1 in Ljubljana. Spend Full Day #1 there. Walk around, see the castle, soak in the hipster city vibes.

Spend Night 2 in Ljubljana, too. Then on the second full day, take a day trip down to Predjama and Skocjan (and/or Postojna). You can knock both of those out in a day, no problem. I think they're each about an hour from Ljubljana. Spend Night 3 in Ljubljana.

Morning of Full Day 3, drive to Bled (less than an hour). Spend nights 4 and 5 in Ljubljana. See the lake (take a row boat to the island/church); see the castle; see Tito's old vacation home; walk the circumference of the lake; go see Vintgar Gorge (seriously -- often overlooked but beautiful). While you're there, if you're able to -- depends on how on-the-go you want to be -- drive into Triglav National Park to see Lake Bohinj.

Maribor is a great area to visit if you like wine. Slovenia has a winemaking culture and history that predates the Romans. (I have not been to Maribor myself but want to and did an amazing Slovenian wine tasting in Bled last year -- happy to share the name of the company if interested!)

A lot of people spend only a day in Bled but I'd give it more. For a small area there's lots to see and do. Get the cream cake at Kavarna Park or Villa Bled. At least 3 days stationed in Bled with day trips is a must I think (it's really well connected to other parts of the country and imo just a really pleasant area to base oneself in, no need to move around every night when things are so close).

I did a day tour of Triglav National Park, the Julian Alps, Lago del Predil, the Soca valley/river, Vrsic Pass, and Lake Jasna. Amazing views at each!

Ljubljana is doable in a day but again it's really nice to wander the old town so you can stretch it out for however long you want. The square has a lot of fun street musicians in the evening and lots of places to get a spritz near the canal.

Mid 20s is "cool" for you? Well, cool. You can expect that in the lower areas. In the mountains its cooler (but the sun burns hotter).

I think Slovenia is still more affordable than Austria.

Public transport is reliable in both countries. Trains are extremely slow (but nice) in Slovenia, buses are okay. Austria is a bit more organized, with all timetables in oebb.at, I am not sure if Slovenia has such a system in place.

Remote locations may not be connected to public transportation in both countries. Austria may have special hiking buses in popular mountain locations, I haven't heard of that in Slovenia.

In Slovenia expect crowds in Bled and Postojna and basically nowhere else. Around Mt Triglav you won't be the only hiker and in Bovec you won't be the only rafter, but 'crowds'? Not really. Austria does not have that many overcrowded places either, but its tourist highlights are more famous/crowded.

Of course each country has enough to do for 2 weeks. What do you want to do?

Just want to note that some people will come and tell you not to go to Hallstatt, that it's overrun and not that amazing. While it's overrun, it still is beautiful and definitely worth a visit.

Take the train to the train station "Hallstatt". It's situated on the opposite side of the lake, so you need to take the boat to go to Hallstatt. Ticket available at the boat.

This way you'll have a magical arrival into Hallstatt, compared to taking a bus which goes via a tunnel and ends on a big, uncharming parking lot.

Also check out lake Vorderer Gosausee, reachable by bus from Hallstatt.

Or also lake Altaussee or lake Grundlsee. All of them are close to Hallstatt. Check on Google Maps how to reach it and if your travel schedule allows it.

There are many more hidden gems in the area (Wolfgangsee, Mondsee, Attersee, Gmunden, Traunsee, etc etc), but having a car would make those places more accessible

For Vienna:
There’s the Naschmarkt, but it has become quite a tourist location as well, so you might consider brunnenmarkt instead for Markets. Unless it’s Saturday, then go to the Naschmarkt because there’s always a flea market as well.
there’s the Donaukanal in vienna where graffiti is allowed/even encouraged which has thus basically become sort of a gallery of graffiti/streetart. Based on what you’re writing you might enjoy it. It is also right next to the inner city (at Schwedenplatz you’ll get the best icecream) and next to the second district which is the former Jewish Quarter of Vienna.
The 7th district is the most known as the hipster district afaik, so this is where you go for vegan/vegetarian cusine. Having been vegetarian basically my entire life though, nowadays almost any place will serve vegetarian food, most even have a few options.
a very local experience in general is the Vienna Kaffeehauskultur. If you want a rather fancy experience, I‘d recommend the cafe Diglas im Schottenstift. It’s very nice, good atmosphere, sometimes even someone playing the piano while still not being overcrowded like some of the super typical „must see“ cafes that have become totally overpriced. If you want the more local experience, my dad would surely recommend the cafe Benedict, which I would describe as still typical but a bit more rustic. Another option is aida - which is a Kaffeehaus-chain found in many places in vienna. It has a distinct very pink and out-of-date design. I personally don’t like it, but it is definitely also something typical.
since it’s something I do a lot: there are many small mainly original-language cinemas in Vienna in case that is something you like.

One annoyance, I only booked places with air conditioning and it turned out that NONE of the places actually had an AC - in August it was hot in some places (obv not the higher elevations) and some places I booked didn’t have window screens, so it was get eaten alive by mosquitoes (and of course I have a mosquito allergy) or lose weight via sweat. I thought some of the tourist attractions in Slovenia were underdeveloped and priced too high for what they offered. I always get negative comments when I write about this experience/perspective in Slovenia, so obviously that was just my experience, there were many things I loved about Slovenia, like the cable ride up the mountain and bee keeping museum, kayaking and hiking and touring a 400 year old original black kitchen.
